knownFor: Bishop of Rome from 366 or 367 after an election fought with clubs and swords, whose councils held to the creed of Nicaea, and who set Jerome of Strido to revise the Latin Gospels.
datesNote: Bishop from 366, by the date of the Ursinian account kept in the Collectio Avellana, or 367, by Jerome of Strido's Chronicle as A. C. Zenos cites it; died in the reign of Theodosius at almost eighty, by Jerome's account

traces: At his request Jerome of Strido revised the old Latin Gospels against the Greek. Jerome's preface begins, "You urge me to revise the old Latin version."
Jerome says that he helped Damasus with his letters and wrote his answers to the councils of the East and West.
In his preface Jerome says he expects to be called a forger and a profane person for revising the old Latin version. Fremantle dates the preface to 383.
A verse of his at the place in the catacombs where Peter and Paul were said to have lain says that the East sent them as disciples, but that Rome deserved rather to defend them as her citizens.
In the sixth century Pope Vigilius set up an inscription honoring martyrs whom, it says, Damasus found and marked with a poem.
Sozomen, in the next century, retells the law of 380 as bringing all the emperor's subjects to the faith that Peter had preached to the Romans and that Damasus and Peter of Alexandria professed.

Theodoret tells that at Antioch, when the general Sapor showed the imperial edict, the priest Flavian told two rival bishops to show that they agreed with Damasus, and told Apollinarius to embrace the teaching of Damasus.
About 449, in his own quarrel, Theodoret quotes Damasus's anathema against those who say that pain on the cross was borne by the Godhead and not by the body with the soul. The date is the editor's.

Eastern bishops, in a letter to Rufus kept by Theodoret, write that the points they list are those for which "the thrice blessed Damasus deposed the heretics Apollinarius, Vitalius, and Timotheus." The held text gives no date.
The Roman Breviary of 1908 keeps his feast on 11 December.
remembered: Jerome, writing to him from the East in 376 or 377, said he kept communion with none but Damasus, "that is with the chair of Peter."
In his Lives of Illustrious Men, Jerome remembers that he "had a fine talent for making verses and published many brief works in heroic metre."

Ammianus Marcellinus, a historian and most likely a pagan, set the riot of his election beside a sharp picture of Rome's bishops, "enriched by offerings from matrons, riding in carriages, dressing splendidly."
Blomfield Jackson, who translated Theodoret, quotes Northcote and Brownlow on his work in the catacombs, "to rediscover the tombs which had been blocked up for concealment under Diocletian."
The book of the popes' lives says he was buried on the Via Ardeatina, in his own basilica, on 11 December, beside his mother and his sister.

uncertain: Ammianus Marcellinus blames both rivals and counts a hundred and thirty-seven dead in the Basilica of Sicininus in one day. Socrates of Constantinople blames Ursinus, who had himself ordained in secret. Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, tells it the same way after him. An anonymous account from Ursinus's own party, kept in the Collectio Avellana, blames Damasus. It says he paid charioteers, arena men and gravediggers, and counts a hundred and sixty dead in a church he besieged, none on his side.

The Avellana account dates Liberius's death and the fighting by the consuls of 366, and Chester Hartranft, who translated Sozomen, dates Liberius's death to September 366. A. C. Zenos, who translated Socrates, notes that Jerome's Chronicle puts it in 367.

The chronological tables in W. H. Fremantle's translation of Jerome's works date his death to December 384. Ernest Cushing Richardson, who translated Jerome's Lives, gives 380 in a note. Jerome himself says only that he died under Theodosius, at almost eighty.
Zenos's note calls him "a Spaniard by race, native of Mantua". No early witness in the sources used here gives his birthplace.
Sozomen calls his rival Ursicius. Ammianus, Socrates and the Avellana account call him Ursinus.

Ammianus says the city's governor, Juventius, could not stop the disorders and was forced by the violence to withdraw to the suburbs. He says later that Praetextatus, as governor, appeased a tumult that the quarrels of the Christians had raised, and that after Ursinus was expelled calm was restored.

Jerome's Chronicle says Ursinus, made bishop by some, seized the Sicininum with his men, and that when Damasus's people flocked there the most cruel killings of both sexes followed. Rufinus says Ursinus, a deacon, had a rustic and unskilled bishop ordain him in the basilica of Sicininus, and that the prefect Maximinus turned the matter against a good and innocent priest, even to the torture of clergy. Socrates says the dispute was not about any article of faith but only about who should be bishop, and that many clergy and laity were punished by the prefect Maximin.

The Ursinian account says Damasus paid the judge of the city and the prefect of the grain supply to have Ursinus and two deacons exiled, and that after the exile he fell with armed followers on worshippers gathered at St Agnes and struck down many. It says the crowd chanted that Damasus had made a fifth war, and that the matrons loved him so much that he was called the matrons' ear-tickler. The clubs and swords of the fight are in this account only; Ammianus says only that the partisans carried their violence to actual battle. The account calls the besieged church the basilica of Liberius, while Jerome and Rufinus put the fighting at the Sicininum, and the held texts do not settle whether these are one building.

The Liber Pontificalis says a council of priests chose Damasus and that Ursinus was made bishop of Naples. Duchesne judges those lines a later addition modeled on the story of Pope Symmachus, and says Ursinus never held another see. Blomfield Jackson's note calls Damasus the nominee of the Arian party; no held ancient text says so.

An order of the emperors to Praetextatus, on the petition of the defenders of the Roman church or of Damasus, has the one church still held by dissenters opened to Damasus. Günther dates it between 16 November 367 and 12 January 368.

The council at Rome that cut off Auxentius of Milan also annulled the decrees of Rimini, on the plea that the bishop of Rome had not assented to them. The year 369 is Hartranft's note. Jackson notes that the Latin of the council's letter differs materially from the Greek Theodoret gives.

Rufinus says Apollinaris at first taught that the Lord took a body but no soul, and, when pressed, said he had a soul but not its reasoning part, which the Word of God itself filled. Hartranft's note gives the year of the council at Rome that condemned him as 377 by Rade or 374 by Hefele.

Basil, in a letter without an address, asks the bishop of Rome to send help to the East; the Benedictine editors say it was obviously addressed to Damasus. In another letter Basil writes of the West: "Really lofty souls, when they are courted, get haughtier than ever." That this is aimed at Damasus is Ceillier's reading, as Jackson reports it, from Basil's wish to write to their Coryphaeus.

Günther dates the emperors' rescript on Damasus's court, to the vicar Aquilinus, between 9 August 378 and 19 January 379. It also sends a metropolitan's case to Rome, or to judges the bishop of Rome names. Duchesne dates to 380 the letter of a Roman council to the emperors that asks for such an order.

That letter from the council says the party of Ursinus set up Isaac, a Jew, whose accusation sought Damasus's head, and that the emperors, by their judgment, found Damasus innocent. Duchesne judges the Liber Pontificalis's charge of adultery modeled on the story of Symmachus, and says Damasus was then about seventy-five. The nature of the charge is not known.

Duchesne says that the tradition of which tomb was whose had already grown obscure or confused by the end of the fourth century, so that the church had to work to establish the identity of the holy tombs. The sources give no reason for the searching out of the graves.

briefReferences: Jerome, Against John of Jerusalem 8: Praetextatus's joke to Damasus. Jerome gives no date for the saying.
Ammianus, Roman History 27.3 and 27.9: the two rival parties, the battle, the 137 dead in the Basilica of Sicininus; Praetextatus as governor appeasing the tumult, and Ursinus expelled.
The account from Ursinus's party, in the Collectio Avellana: Damasus's paid charioteers, arena fighters and gravediggers, and the 160 dead, men and women, with none on Damasus's side.
Jerome's Chronicle, Rufinus, Socrates 4.29 and Sozomen 6.23: the church writers who blame Ursinus.
Sozomen 6.23, with Hartranft's note, and Theodoret's text of the council's letter: the council at Rome that cut off Auxentius of Milan, and the year 369.
Theodoret, Church History 4.19: the letter of the bishop of Alexandria, and the deacon sent with Damasus's letters led bound and flogged.
Rufinus, Church History 10, and Sozomen 6.25: Damasus and the bishop of Alexandria condemn Apollinaris in council at Rome. Damasus's letter in Theodoret: the judgment of the apostolic see.
Theodoret, Church History 5.2: the edict after Valens died, handing the churches to those in communion with Damasus, and the general sent to enforce it.
The emperors' rescript to the vicar Aquilinus, in the Collectio Avellana: a bishop condemned by Damasus with a council of five or seven bishops, who holds on to his church, is sent to Rome.

Theodosian Code 16.1.2, the edict of 27 February 380, in Latin: the faith Peter handed down, and Damasus and Peter of Alexandria as its measure; those who do not follow it bear the infamy of heretical teaching.
The petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus, in the Collectio Avellana: Macarius, and the judge acting as if under an imperial rescript. The petition gives no date and cites no law.
The Liber Pontificalis, with Duchesne: the searching out of the martyrs' graves and the verses, in a book written about 150 years later.

Jerome, preface to the Four Gospels, tr. Fremantle: the request to revise the old Latin version. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 103, and Fremantle's tables: Damasus almost eighty at his death, in December 384.
His epitaph, from De Rossi as printed in Duchesne's Liber Pontificalis: the sea's bitter waves, the brother given back to his sister Martha, and the last line.
World census, Imperial and Juridical Christianity: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: Make me bishop of the city of Rome, and I will be a Christian at once.
quotationOriginals.printed: Make me bishop of Rome, and I will at once be a Christian.
quotationOriginals.work: Jerome, Against John of Jerusalem 8, tr. W. H. Fremantle, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 6
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Jerome's Latin, in Migne's Patrologia Latina 23 (lines 27958-27960 of its file), is damaged at the name of the city: the scan prints Πο- mans for Romanae. Mansi's print of the same sentence (lines 42056-42058 of its file) reads Romane urbis, so the Latin is bishop of the city of Rome, and the modern wording follows it. The English print stands alone. Jerome reports the saying as one Praetextatus made in jest, without a date, after Praetextatus had died as consul designate.

quotationOriginals.modern: It is our will that all the peoples under our merciful rule live in the religion that the divine apostle Peter handed down to the Romans. The faith he brought them, kept to this day, shows that he did. It is plain that Bishop Damasus follows it, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, a man of an apostle's holiness.
quotationOriginals.printed: cunctos populos, quos clementiae nostrae regit temperamentum, in tali volumus religione versari, quam divinum petrum apostolum tradidisse romanis religio usque ad nunc ab ipso insinuata declarat quamque pontificem damasum sequi claret et petrum alexandriae episcopum virum apostolicae sanctitatis
quotationOriginals.work: Edict of Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius to the people of Constantinople, 27 February 380, Theodosian Code 16.1.2, Latin
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Latin Library does not say which edition it follows. Mommsen and Meyer's critical text (lines 83597-83601 of its file, whose scan prints Cuncios for Cunctos) reads the same words. The modern wording renders pontificem as bishop. The Latin goes on to say that this is to believe in one Godhead of Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the quotation stops before that.

quotationOriginals.modern: I believe that, after the ashes, he will make Damasus rise.
quotationOriginals.printed: post cineres Damasum faciet quia surgere credo.
quotationOriginals.work: Epitaph of Damasus, verses that Duchesne takes to be his own, from De Rossi, in Duchesne's Liber Pontificalis
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Duchesne's print is the only one the Library holds, and its scan is damaged in the poem's second and fourth lines (128206 and 128210); this last line reads cleanly. Duchesne says the verses were composed by Damasus himself. The one who will make Damasus rise is the one the poem's earlier lines describe: who walked and stilled the sea's bitter waves, who could loose the deadly chains of death, and who gave a brother back to his sister Martha.
